extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers and experimental scientists (readers/members of the Royal Society, 17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and publishing empirical observations and experiments (astronomical, anatomical, microscopical, surgical, and mathematical) as communicated to a learned society, including methods, instruments, and results. Emphasizes procedural detail, replication, and comparison with prior authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed procedural description of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the exact procedure used in experiments (materials, how applied, sequence of operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: applying 'a button-pledget of lint dipped in the liquor' to a cut vessel, keeping it on 'about a quarter of an hour', changing pledgets when necessary, and describing how compresses were applied in limb amputations. The account specifies modes of application (in the mouth, nostrils), preparations (lint, pledget), and stepwise actions taken during trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record precise timings and quantitative observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the durations and measurable outcomes of procedures and trials (times to staunch bleeding, elongations, weights, powder amounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reports give explicit times: 'staunched in 7 min.', 'in less than half a quarter of an hour', 'kept on by the pressure of the thumb about a quarter of an hour'. For ordnance tests the exact weights of cannon, bullets, and powder used are reported (e.g., demy cannon 34 cwt, bullet 34 lbs, powder 12–24 lbs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication and repetition of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat trials and report repeated outcomes across specimens, occasions, and locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes repeating experiments: 'these experiments having so well succeeded on brutes, and been repeated over and over with the like success', and reports trials at different places (London, Whitehall, Paris) and by different operators (Mr. Wiseman, Dr. Needham, Denys himself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression from animal trials to human trials with documented results
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with animal experiments, then proceed to human applications, documenting effects and adverse outcomes (or lack thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account describes testing the styptic first on dogs (cutting crural and carotid arteries), then on men (temporal arteries opened, hands and face cut), and reports outcomes in both groups, including survival and healing without ligature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report healing outcomes and possible adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: State not only immediate effects but also subsequent healing, presence/absence of suppuration, scarring, or other complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denys's claim: the remedy 'stops the blood instantly without any need of binding up the wound... healing without any scar, suppuration, or cicatrice.' Experiments explicitly note the absence of suppuration and cicatrice and that wounds 'healed without any ill accident.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide instrumentation, station, and accommodation details for observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify observing stations, instruments, assistants, and accommodations necessary for reliable observations (especially astronomical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed states that observations made 'from a more convenient station' are more accurate and that, had he 'a convenient place for observing, a ready assistant, and other necessary accommodations' he could rectify star catalog errors. This implies that reports should describe observational circumstances and available resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give measurements and note anomalies; state uncertainty and propose further trials
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering anomalies or potential errors, describe them candidly, quantify the inconsistency, and propose additional trials to confirm or refute the observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed notes 'I have just cause to suspect some eccentricity in the third [satellite]' and 'I intend, at another opportunity, to make more trials as carefully as I can, either to confirm or destroy this observation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply drawings/figures for anatomical and microscopical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Include illustrations or drawings to accompany detailed anatomical descriptions to aid verification and further investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swammerdam 'transmit[ted] to the Society a drawing' of the scarabaeus nasicornis genital organs with detailed measurements ('a single tube, 2 feet 6 inches long') and structures; the text explicitly relies on these drawings to communicate the finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple-lens microscopy and meticulous instrument preparation to avoid artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use carefully ground single lenses and meticulous preparation of microscopes to reduce optical deception and obtain reliable microscopical observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leewenhoek 'applied himself with unremitted care to the grinding and polishing into a state of perfection the simple lens' as 'being the best calculated for accurate investigation' and 'less liable to those deceptions which a composition of glasses sometimes occasions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe new instruments with parts and instructions for use
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing instruments, give a description of their parts and the method of using them so readers can reproduce and employ them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S. Moreland 'gives us here both a description of the parts and structure of these instruments, and the way and manner of using them' (for addition/subtraction and multiplication instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstrations should be built from clear lemmas and logical steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the underlying lemmas or elementary results that support a general mathematical method, and show how they combine to yield the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Slusius enumerates lemmas used in his method: e.g., 'The difference of two powers of the same degree, divided by the difference of their roots, gives the several members of the next inferior power of their binomial', and lists other foundational observations as the basis for drawing tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite prior authorities and compare new results with established observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference classical and contemporary sources and compare current observations against them to situate novelty and correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions invoke Cicero, Hero, Vitruvius, Cassini, Townley, Malpighi, Needham, and Tycho; criticisms and comparative assessments (e.g., superiority of ancient music or disagreement with Cassini's satellite elongations) are used to argue or contextualize claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors may omit raw data judged not useful but should state the omission
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor can omit certain data from a communication if not currently useful, but should note the omission for transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial remark: 'The observations are omitted, as not now of any use.' This signals a practice of selective publication with explicit justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cautionary limitations and conventional safeguards for clinical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting medical or surgical remedies, include caveats and prevailing surgical safeguards where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A footnote warns that although various styptics have been proposed, for bleeding from a puncture or division of a large artery 'no remedy can be safely trusted to, but that of passing a ligature round the ruptured or divided vessel.' This shows including conventional cautions alongside novel claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate practical comparative advantages with empirical tests
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming improvements (e.g., in metallurgy, instruments, or music), present empirical tests and examples showing comparative advantage (efficiency, material saving, strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The powder for rendering metal 'makes the metal so close and smooth... One third of the metal may be spared' and firing tests ('demy cannon... tried with a bullet of 34 lbs... employed 12–24 lbs of strong powder... indured very well') are presented as evidence of practical advantage.
